LPIC-1 Section 10 Scenario-Based IT Engineering Lab Guide
Objectives 104.5 and 104.6: Manage file permissions and ownership, and create and change hard and symbolic links, using realistic access tickets, audits, and release changes.

Treat each lab like an access ticket or an audit finding, not a chmod drill. Read the scenario, decide who needs what access, make the smallest change that delivers it, and prove the result from the command line with ls -l, stat, or a test that should fail.

Use a Linux Mint VM and stay inside ~/lpic1-section10. Never change permissions or owners on system files under /etc, /usr, or /var; the audit labs only read them. A few steps need sudo, and each one says so. The sticky bit lab works in its own folder under /tmp and removes it at the end.
Step 1: Check which groups you belong to. On Linux Mint the first user created at install is normally a member of the adm group, which several labs use:
If adm is not in the list, use sudo in front of the chgrp and chown commands that name adm.
Step 3: Create the sample files and give them the starting permissions the labs expect:
chmod 666 deploy/db.credentials; chmod 644 deploy/deploy.sh logs/health.log; chmod 777 releases/app-1.0/app.conf

Validation check: Run ls -lR and confirm deploy, logs, and releases contain the files above, and that db.credentials shows -rw-rw-rw-. If a lab goes wrong, rerun Step 3 to reset the files and their modes.

ls -l, ls -ld, ls -i, ls -li, stat, file, whoami, id, id -u, id -g, id -gn, id -G, id -Gn, groups, getent group, chown, chown user:group, chown :group, chown -R, chgrp, chgrp -R, chmod, chmod u+x, chmod go=, chmod a=r, chmod u=rwX,go=rX, chmod 640, chmod 4755, chmod 2775, chmod 1777, chmod u+s, chmod g+s, chmod o+t, umask, umask -S, umask 027, mkfifo, find -perm, find -type, find -samefile, find -xtype l, ln, ln -s, ln -sf, ln -sfn, readlink, readlink -f, and sudo -u.

Read a mode as one type character plus three triplets: user, group, other, each in the order r, w, x. In octal, r is 4, w is 2, and x is 1, so 7 is everything and 0 is nothing. A fourth digit in front adds the special bits: 4 for SUID, 2 for SGID, and 1 for sticky. The umask is what gets taken away from 666 for files and 777 for directories. A hard link is a second name for the same inode; a symbolic link is a small file that holds a path.
Beginner Labs: Reading Permissions and Ownership

title: Lab 1: Decode a long listing for a security audit
scenario: An auditor flags the deploy folder and asks for the exact mode, owner, and group of every file in it, in both letters and numbers.
task: Produce a listing of the deploy and logs folders and of the deploy directory itself, then add the octal modes.
deliverable: reports/listing.txt with ls and stat output.
steps: ls -l deploy logs > reports/listing.txt
ls -ld deploy >> reports/listing.txt
stat -c '%A %a %U %G %n' deploy/* logs/* >> reports/listing.txt
validation: cat reports/listing.txt and confirm db.credentials shows -rw-rw-rw- and 666. That is the audit finding: anyone on the system can read and change the database password.
trap: ls -l on a directory lists what is inside it. Add -d to see the directory's own mode and owner. The number after the mode is the link count, not a size.

title: Lab 2: Identify every file type in an inventory
scenario: A junior engineer asks why some entries in /dev and /run start with b, c, s, or p instead of a dash or d.
task: Create a named pipe and a symbolic link in the lab folder, find examples of the other types on the system, and list them together.
deliverable: reports/file-types.txt with one example of each type, and reports/file-cmd.txt with what the file command says about three of them.
steps: mkfifo work.pipe; ln -s logs/health.log latest.log
ls -ld logs/health.log logs work.pipe latest.log /dev/null > reports/file-types.txt
find /dev -maxdepth 1 -type b | head -2 | xargs -r ls -l >> reports/file-types.txt
find /run -maxdepth 2 -type s 2>/dev/null | head -2 | xargs -r ls -l >> reports/file-types.txt
file /dev/null work.pipe latest.log > reports/file-cmd.txt
validation: cut -c1 reports/file-types.txt | sort | uniq -c and confirm you see -, d, l, p, c, b, and s.
trap: The type codes are - regular file, d directory, l symbolic link, b block device, c character device, p named pipe (FIFO), and s socket. Disks are block devices; terminals and /dev/null are character devices.

title: Lab 3: Confirm your identity and groups before an access ticket
scenario: A ticket says you cannot read a file owned by the adm group. Before changing anything, the team lead wants proof of who you are and which groups you are in.
task: Record your user name, your UID and GIDs, your primary group, and the members of adm.
steps: whoami > reports/identity.txt
id >> reports/identity.txt
id -gn >> reports/identity.txt; id -Gn >> reports/identity.txt; groups >> reports/identity.txt
getent group adm >> reports/identity.txt
validation: cat reports/identity.txt and confirm the id -gn line matches your user name and that adm appears in the id -Gn and groups lines.
trap: id -g shows only the primary (effective) group; id -G shows all of them. A group you were just added to does not apply until you log in again or run newgrp, so a fresh membership can look like it is not working.

title: Lab 4: Change the group and owner of a log file
scenario: Log reviewers in the adm group need to read logs/health.log, and the security team wants the file owned by root during a review. Afterwards it goes back to you.
task: Change the group with chgrp, change the owner with chown, change both at once, and then return the file to yourself.
deliverable: reports/ownership.txt showing the owner and group after each change.
steps: chgrp adm logs/health.log; ls -l logs/health.log > reports/ownership.txt
sudo chown root logs/health.log; ls -l logs/health.log >> reports/ownership.txt
sudo chown root:adm logs/health.log; ls -l logs/health.log >> reports/ownership.txt
sudo chown $USER:$USER logs/health.log; ls -l logs/health.log >> reports/ownership.txt
chown :adm logs/health.log; ls -l logs/health.log >> reports/ownership.txt
validation: cat reports/ownership.txt and follow the owner and group columns through all five lines. The last line shows you as owner and adm as group.
trap: Only root can give a file to another user, so chown needs sudo. You can change the group of a file you own without sudo, but only to a group you belong to. chown :group changes just the group, and chown user: sets the group to that user's login group.

title: Lab 5: Lock down a credentials file with symbolic mode
scenario: Follow-up to the audit in Lab 1: db.credentials must be readable and writable only by its owner, and deploy.sh must be executable by its owner.
task: Fix both files with symbolic chmod, one change at a time, and record the mode after each change.
steps: chmod o-w deploy/db.credentials; stat -c '%a %A %n' deploy/db.credentials > reports/symbolic.txt
chmod go= deploy/db.credentials; stat -c '%a %A %n' deploy/db.credentials >> reports/symbolic.txt
chmod u+x deploy/deploy.sh; stat -c '%a %A %n' deploy/deploy.sh >> reports/symbolic.txt
Practice on a scratch copy: cp deploy/deploy.sh reports/scratch.sh, then try chmod a=x, chmod u=rw,go=r, and chmod ug+w,o-r on it, checking with ls -l after each one.
validation: cat reports/symbolic.txt and confirm the lines read 664, then 600 -rw-------, then 744 -rwxr--r--.
trap: u means the user who owns the file, and o means other, not owner. = sets the level to exactly what you list, so go= removes everything from group and other. a=x leaves only execute everywhere.

title: Lab 6: Set standard modes with octal numbers
scenario: The team standard for the deploy area is: scripts 750, logs 640, credentials 600, and the deploy directory 750.
task: Apply the standard with octal chmod and prove each mode.
steps: chmod 750 deploy/deploy.sh deploy; chmod 640 logs/health.log; chmod 600 deploy/db.credentials
stat -c '%a %A %n' deploy deploy/* logs/health.log > reports/octal.txt
Work out these by hand, then check them on reports/scratch.sh: 764, 755, 644, 000, and back to 644.
validation: cat reports/octal.txt and confirm 750 drwxr-x---, 750 -rwxr-x---, 600 -rw-------, and 640 -rw-r-----.
trap: Octal mode always sets all three levels at once; there is no octal way to change just the group. Any digit that includes execute is odd. A leading 0, as in 0644, means no special bits and is the same as 644.

title: Lab 7: Explain why a user can list a folder but not open its files
scenario: A ticket says: I can see the file names in the handoff folder, but every file says Permission denied. Another user can open a file by name but cannot list the folder.
task: Reproduce both complaints on a test folder by changing r, w, and x on the directory, then restore it.
deliverable: reports/dir-perms.txt with the errors you reproduced.
steps: mkdir -p shared/handoff; echo 'call db01 owner' > shared/handoff/note.txt
chmod u=rw shared/handoff; ls shared/handoff > reports/dir-perms.txt 2>&1; cat shared/handoff/note.txt >> reports/dir-perms.txt 2>&1
chmod u=x shared/handoff; ls shared/handoff >> reports/dir-perms.txt 2>&1; cat shared/handoff/note.txt >> reports/dir-perms.txt 2>&1
chmod u=rx shared/handoff; touch shared/handoff/new.txt >> reports/dir-perms.txt 2>&1
chmod 755 shared/handoff
validation: cat reports/dir-perms.txt. With rw- the names list but cat is denied; with --x cat works but ls is denied; with r-x touch is denied.
trap: On a directory, r lists names, x lets you enter it and reach files inside, and w lets you create, rename, and delete entries. Deleting a file depends on the directory's w, not on the file's own mode.

title: Lab 8: Fix modes and ownership across a whole release tree
scenario: A release was copied from a USB stick and the modes are a mess: one config is 777. Directories must be 755 and files 644, and the tree must be owned by root:adm while operations reviews it.
task: Fix the tree recursively without making plain files executable, then hand it back to yourself.
steps: chmod -R u=rwX,go=rX releases
find releases -type d -exec chmod 755 {} + ; find releases -type f -exec chmod 644 {} +
sudo chown -R root:adm releases; find releases -printf '%m %u:%g %p\n' > reports/releases-perms.txt
sudo chown -R $USER: releases
validation: cat reports/releases-perms.txt and confirm every directory is 755, every file is 644, and every line shows root:adm.
trap: chmod -R 755 would make every file executable. Capital X adds execute only to directories and to files that already have execute for someone, which is why the 777 config came out 755 after the first step and needed the find step. chgrp -R and chown -R work the same way recursively.

title: Lab 9: Diagnose new files that come out group-writable
scenario: A security review asks why new files you create are group-writable, and wants to see what a stricter umask would produce.
task: Record your umask, then create test files and folders under umask 027 and 077 without changing your session's umask.
steps: umask > reports/umask.txt; umask -S >> reports/umask.txt
touch reports/u-default.txt; mkdir reports/u-default.dir
(umask 027; touch reports/u027.txt; mkdir reports/u027.dir)
(umask 077; touch reports/u077.txt; mkdir reports/u077.dir)
stat -c '%a %n' reports/u-default.* reports/u027.* reports/u077.* >> reports/umask.txt
validation: cat reports/umask.txt. With Mint's default umask 0002 you should see 664 and 775, then 640 and 750, then 600 and 700. If your umask differs, work out the expected modes first. Run umask again to confirm your session's value did not change.
trap: New files start from 666 and directories from 777, and the umask removes bits from those. A umask never adds execute to a new file. The parentheses run umask in a subshell, so the change disappears when it ends. 027 and 0027 mean the same thing.

Advanced Labs: Special Permissions and Links

title: Lab 10: Audit SUID and SGID programs
scenario: A compliance scan wants the list of programs that run with their owner's or group's privileges, plus an explanation of why passwd needs it.
task: Find SUID and SGID files in the system binary folders, and record the modes of passwd and /tmp. This lab only reads.
steps: ls -l /usr/bin/passwd > reports/suid-audit.txt; ls -ld /tmp >> reports/suid-audit.txt
find /usr/bin /usr/sbin -type f -perm -4000 2>/dev/null >> reports/suid-audit.txt
echo '--- SGID ---' >> reports/suid-audit.txt; find /usr/bin /usr/sbin -type f -perm -2000 2>/dev/null >> reports/suid-audit.txt
validation: grep -E 'passwd|/tmp' reports/suid-audit.txt shows -rwsr-xr-x on passwd and drwxrwxrwt on /tmp.
trap: passwd is SUID root so an ordinary user can update /etc/shadow, which only root can write. -perm -4000 means at least the SUID bit is set; -perm /6000 matches SUID or SGID.

title: Lab 11: Build a team folder with SGID and a drop folder with the sticky bit
scenario: The ops team wants a shared folder where every new file belongs to the adm group automatically, and a public drop folder where people cannot delete each other's files.
task: Set SGID on a lab folder and prove the group is inherited, then prove the sticky bit stops another user from deleting your file.
steps: mkdir shared/ops; chgrp adm shared/ops; chmod 2775 shared/ops; touch shared/ops/runbook.txt shared/plain.txt
ls -ld shared/ops > reports/team-folders.txt; ls -l shared/ops/runbook.txt shared/plain.txt >> reports/team-folders.txt
mkdir /tmp/lpic1-drop; chmod 1777 /tmp/lpic1-drop; echo mine > /tmp/lpic1-drop/mine.txt
sudo -u nobody rm -f /tmp/lpic1-drop/mine.txt >> reports/team-folders.txt 2>&1; ls /tmp/lpic1-drop >> reports/team-folders.txt
chmod o-t /tmp/lpic1-drop; sudo -u nobody rm -f /tmp/lpic1-drop/mine.txt >> reports/team-folders.txt 2>&1; ls -A /tmp/lpic1-drop | wc -l >> reports/team-folders.txt
rm -r /tmp/lpic1-drop
validation: cat reports/team-folders.txt. shared/ops shows drwxrwsr-x, runbook.txt has group adm while plain.txt does not, the first rm by nobody says Operation not permitted, and the last count is 0 because without the sticky bit nobody could delete your file.
trap: SGID on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group; SGID on a program makes it run with the program's group. The sticky bit on a directory means only the file's owner, the directory's owner, or root can delete or rename a file in it.

title: Lab 12: Read and set special bits in octal, including the capital S and T
scenario: A reviewer sees rwSr--r-- on a script and asks whether SUID is working. You need to show the difference between lowercase and capital letters.
task: Set special bits in octal on test files and a test directory and record the results.
steps: touch reports/sp-a reports/sp-b reports/sp-c reports/sp-d; mkdir reports/sp-dir reports/sp-dir2
chmod 4644 reports/sp-a; chmod 4755 reports/sp-b; chmod 2750 reports/sp-c; chmod 6755 reports/sp-d; chmod 1777 reports/sp-dir; chmod 1770 reports/sp-dir2
stat -c '%a %A %n' reports/sp-* > reports/special-bits.txt
chmod u-s,g-s reports/sp-d; chmod o-t reports/sp-dir; stat -c '%a %A %n' reports/sp-d reports/sp-dir >> reports/special-bits.txt
validation: cat reports/special-bits.txt and match: 4644 rwSr--r--, 4755 rwsr-xr-x, 2750 rwxr-s---, 6755 rwsr-sr-x, 1777 rwxrwxrwt, 1770 rwxrwx--T, then 755 and 777 after the removals.
trap: A capital S or T means the special bit is set but the matching execute bit is missing, so it has no effect. With GNU chmod, a plain numeric mode such as 755 does not clear SGID on a directory; use chmod g-s, or a five-digit mode such as 00755.

title: Lab 13: Give a log a second name with hard and symbolic links
scenario: Monitoring reads logs/health-soft.log and a cleanup script reads logs/health-hard.log, but both must see the same data as logs/health.log. Then someone deletes the original by mistake.
task: Create a hard link and a symbolic link, compare them, delete the original, and see which name survives.
steps: ln logs/health.log logs/health-hard.log; ln -s health.log logs/health-soft.log
ls -li logs > reports/links.txt; stat -c '%i %h %n' logs/health.log logs/health-hard.log >> reports/links.txt
echo 'app02 OK' >> logs/health-hard.log; tail -1 logs/health.log >> reports/links.txt
rm logs/health.log; cat logs/health-hard.log >> reports/links.txt; cat logs/health-soft.log >> reports/links.txt 2>&1
find logs -xtype l >> reports/links.txt; ln logs/health-hard.log logs/health.log; find logs -samefile logs/health.log >> reports/links.txt
validation: cat reports/links.txt. The original and hard link share one inode with a link count of 2, the soft link is type l with an arrow, the hard link still has the data after rm, the soft link says No such file or directory, find -xtype l names it as broken, and after the restore it works again.
trap: A copy gives two names and two sets of data; a hard link gives two names and one set of data. A symbolic link's target is stored as text and resolved from the link's own folder, which is why health.log, not logs/health.log, is the right target here.

title: Lab 14: Switch releases with a symbolic link and test the link limits
scenario: The app reads its config from a current link. Tonight's change moves current from app-1.0 to app-1.1 in one step, and a teammate asks why you did not use a hard link.
task: Point current at app-1.0, switch it to app-1.1 safely, and show the two things hard links cannot do.
steps: ln -s releases/app-1.0 current; readlink current > reports/release-switch.txt
ln -sfn releases/app-1.1 current; readlink current >> reports/release-switch.txt; readlink -f current >> reports/release-switch.txt; cat current/app.conf >> reports/release-switch.txt
ln releases releases-hard >> reports/release-switch.txt 2>&1
ln logs/health.log /dev/shm/health.log >> reports/release-switch.txt 2>&1
ln -s "$PWD/logs/health.log" /dev/shm/health.log; cat /dev/shm/health.log >> reports/release-switch.txt; rm /dev/shm/health.log
validation: cat reports/release-switch.txt and confirm current moved from releases/app-1.0 to releases/app-1.1, the config says version=1.1, the hard link to a directory was refused, and the hard link to /dev/shm failed with Invalid cross-device link while the absolute symlink worked.
trap: Without -n, ln -sf with a link that points to a directory creates the new link inside that directory instead of replacing it. Hard links cannot cross file systems and cannot point to directories; symbolic links can do both, and use an absolute path when the link lives somewhere else.

Reading o as owner. In chmod, u is the owning user, g is the group, o is other (world), and a is all three.
Forgetting that = replaces. chmod g=r removes w and x from the group even if they were set before.
Mixing up the octal values. r is 4, w is 2, x is 1. 6 is rw, 5 is rx, and any odd digit includes execute.
Thinking octal can change one level. chmod 640 always sets owner, group, and other together.
Miscounting four-digit modes. The first digit is the special bits: 4 SUID, 2 SGID, 1 sticky. 6755 is SUID plus SGID.
Treating capital S or T as active. They mean the special bit is set but execute is missing at that level.
Confusing SGID on files and directories. On a program it runs with the file's group; on a directory new files inherit the directory's group.
Expecting the umask to be subtracted from 777 for files. Files start from 666, so umask 022 gives 644 files and 755 directories.
Thinking a non-root user can chown a file to someone else. Only root can change the owner; an owner can only change the group to one of their own groups.
Forgetting the colon forms. chown alice:ops sets both, chown :ops sets only the group, and chown alice: uses alice's login group.
Expecting ls -l dir to show the directory's own mode. Use ls -ld.
Mixing up link counts. A hard link raises the link count of both names; a symbolic link does not change it.
Expecting a symbolic link to survive deleting its target. It dangles; a hard link keeps the data until the last name is removed.
Trying to hard link a directory or across file systems. Both fail; use ln -s instead, and remember ln takes the target first and the new name second.
Complete these tasks without notes. Use only your Linux Mint VM and the files in ~/lpic1-section10. Rerun Step 3 of the Lab Setup first so you start from the original modes.
Record your user name, primary group, and every group you belong to in reports/challenge-id.txt.
Make deploy/db.credentials readable and writable only by its owner using symbolic mode, then prove it with stat.
Set deploy/deploy.sh to 750 with octal mode and logs/health.log to 640.
Fix every mode under releases so directories are 755 and files are 644, without making any file executable.
Create shared/team with group adm so that new files inside it get group adm automatically. Prove it with a test file.
Show, with a subshell, the modes a new file and a new directory get under umask 077, while your own umask stays unchanged.
List every SUID program in /usr/bin and explain in one sentence why passwd is on the list.
Create a hard link and a symbolic link to logs/health.log, delete the original, and show which link still works.
Your final handoff is the reports directory. For each file, write a short sentence explaining what it proves.
Security analyst request: “The database credentials file is world-writable. Make it owner-only and show me the numbers.”
Operations request: “Log reviewers are in the adm group. Give the group read access to the health log and nobody else.”
